terms.comment: The reckoning of an account, then any calculation: Horace’s schoolboys learn their fractions longīs ratiōnibus, by long sums. To do a sum is ratiōnem subdūcere or inīre (Lewis & Short); what it comes to is the summa (see amount).

terms.gloss: a little sum, a small reckoning
terms.comment: In Cicero a petty reason or a quibble (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Lael. 58: ad calculōs vocāre (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The pebble moved on the counting board, and so the reckoning itself: calculōs subdūcere, to work out a sum. See also counter.

evidence: Plaut. Mil. 204: dextera digitīs ratiōnem computat
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: mostly post-Augustan. A reckoning is computātiō (Quint. 1.10.35).

phrases.latin: Beātus videor: subdūxī ratiunculam, quantum aeris mihi sit quantumque aliēnī siet
phrases.english: I feel a happy man: I’ve done a little sum of how much money I have and how much I owe
he is doing a sum on the fingers of his right hand
